Bast fiber.deeper: Bast fibers are hierarchical composites. In flax the elementary fibers are single plant cells with a polygonal cross-section, roughly pentagonal to octagonal, averaging about 15 to 18 micrometers across, each with a thick cellulose-rich secondary wall and a narrow lumen. Pectin and hemicellulose cement overlapping cells into technical bundles, and cellulose microfibrils lie close to the fiber axis, which gives high stiffness and low extension. Composition separates the crops: flax fiber is reported at roughly 64 to 78 percent cellulose with about 2 to 5 percent lignin, long hemp bast at about 55 to 72 percent cellulose and 2 to 5 percent lignin, while jute carries about 12 to 14 percent lignin, which makes it stiffer and prone to yellowing in light. Transverse dislocations called nodes or kink bands help microscopic identification, but flax and hemp are hard to tell apart and laboratories combine drying-twist tests, lignin staining and spectroscopy.
Bast fiber.origins: Bast fibers may be among the oldest textile materials, but the evidence is contested. In 2009 researchers reported fibers from Upper Paleolithic layers of Dzudzuana Cave in the foothills of the Caucasus, Georgia, radiocarbon-dated in part to about 32,000 to 26,000 years before present, and described them as wild flax, some spun, dyed and knotted. A published comment in 2010 argued that microscopy and the presence of nodes were not sufficient to identify the fibers as flax. The exchange illustrates why bast identification still relies on combining several methods.

Carding.deeper: A card works with opposed surfaces clothed in fine wire points. Where two neighboring surfaces carry points that face each other and move at different speeds, tufts are teased apart into individual fibers; where the points trail, fibers are simply stripped from one surface to the next. Cotton cards run a large main cylinder against slowly moving flats, while wool and many nonwoven cards use pairs of worker and stripper rollers around the cylinder. The thin web leaving the card is condensed into sliver for spinning or laid down as a web for nonwoven bonding. Carding also removes some trash and neps, but it cannot remove all short fiber, which is the task of combing. Mill laboratories check the result with single-fiber systems such as AFIS, which reports neps per gram and short fiber content, alongside bundle measurements from the High Volume Instrument.
Carding.origins: Hand cards, paired boards set with bent wire teeth, preceded powered cards, and card rooms later became the dustiest part of cotton mills. Occupational studies linked them to byssinosis: Cavagna and colleagues in 1969 reported the condition in 32 percent of workers in a cotton card room and 47 percent in a hemp card room where airborne bacterial endotoxin was measured, and Rylander and colleagues in 1979 found that Monday lung-function losses among card-room workers in 23 US mills tracked dust levels and, more closely, Gram-negative bacteria in bale cotton. A 1983 analysis found card-room dust richer in noncellulosic organic matter than spinning-room dust.

Chain of custody.deeper: Chain-of-custody systems differ in how tightly the claim follows the physical material. Under segregation, certified material is kept physically apart; under mass balance, certified and uncertified inputs may mix while claims on outputs are capped by verified certified input; under book-and-claim, credits trade without a physical link. The audit logic is a conservation check: over a site boundary and reconciliation period, claimed output must not exceed certified input multiplied by a conversion factor, with losses and carry-over recorded. Textile Exchange's Content Claim Standard 3.0, launched in June 2021, relies on batch-level segregation and limits volume reconciliation to no more than three months. A scope certificate shows that a site is certified; a transaction certificate ties a specific shipment to that status and caps what the next buyer can claim. Laboratory tests can flag problems but cannot prove organic origin, so the documentary chain carries the claim.
Chain of custody.origins: The phrase is borrowed from evidence handling, where every transfer of an item is recorded so its integrity can be shown later. Sustainability schemes adapted the idea for commodities such as palm oil, cocoa and forest products. In textiles, Textile Exchange, which began as Organic Exchange, built chain-of-custody rules around its content standards: the Organic Content Standard carries a 2013 copyright, its version 3.0 is dated 1 March 2020, and the Policy for Transaction Certificates reached version 3.1 on 1 October 2023. The Global Organic Textile Standard also uses transaction certificates.

Combing.deeper: A comber works on a fringe of fibers held in a nipper. Rotating needles comb the free end, then the combed tuft is drawn forward through a stationary top comb that holds back short fibers, neps and trash, and each new tuft is pieced onto the previously combed web. The rejected material is noil. Combing therefore changes the length distribution rather than individual fibers: in cotton, HVI measures bundle upper half mean length and uniformity, and studies report that length, strength and uniformity rise together while short fiber content falls, so removing the short tail makes yarn more even. Evidence from waste-fiber yarns shows the reverse effect: blending in shorter fibers raises mass irregularity, imperfections and hairiness. Removing more noil improves evenness at the cost of yield, the same trade-off that governs flax hackling.
Combing.origins: Combing and hackling share one idea: drawing a fiber mass through pins so that fibers too short to be held are left behind. For flax this was long hand work with hackles, and the Irish Linen Centre and Lisburn Museum holds hackling pins dated to about 1850. In wool, combing defines the worsted route: sliver is gilled and combed, the noil removed and the result formed into top, whereas the woollen route omits combing. In cotton, combing remained an optional step reserved for finer, smoother yarns.
